title: Modular synthetic cross-kingdom promoters enable coordinated expression in Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unzipped the Europe PMC supplement (1.61 MB outer zip). It contains only figure images plus one inner archive holding a 22-page PDF and one spreadsheet, 'Supplementary Table S3-JYL.xlsx' (14 kB). I opened that spreadsheet with openpyxl and dumped every non-empty row: it has 9 unique hybrid promoter names (rows 7-16, with pTDH3C-J23119 listed twice) and columns for the yeast core-promoter sequence, the yeast 5' untranslated region, the E. coli promoter, a spacer, a Shine-Dalgarno sequence, a Kozak sequence and promoter length in base pairs. There is no expression, fluorescence or activity value anywhere in the file. I also pulled the full open-access text and grepped it: 'nine hybrid promoters' appears four times, confirming the design is three yeast core promoters times three E. coli J23 promoters, all measured in biological triplicate.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That mCherry transcript levels, fluorescence intensities and beta-galactosidase activities were measured by flow cytometry and quantitative PCR, and the prodeoxyviolacein pigment titres. Those numbers appear only inside the figure bar graphs (Figures 3-6), which I viewed only as rendered images, not as any data table. The claim that the promoters also work in Corynebacterium glutamicum and Pichia pastoris likewise rests on figures only.

a1_downloadable.note: Supplement downloads freely from Europe PMC with no login: a 1.61 MB zip containing a PDF and one 14 kB spreadsheet. Verified by extracting both.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAILS. The thing a model would predict - promoter strength / expression level - is not a column anywhere. The only spreadsheet contains sequences and lengths; every expression number lives inside bar graphs in the figures, so the label would have to be reconstructed by digitising images.

a3_inputs_present.note: The input side is genuinely fine: full nucleotide sequences for each promoter part are spelled out in the spreadsheet, no accession lookups needed. Verified in the file.

a4_units_stated.note: No units, because there are no measured values in any data file. The figures use relative fluorescence and relative transcript levels; the text never states an absolute unit. Verified by searching the full text for 'arbitrary unit', 'RFU' and 'a.u.' - zero hits.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS badly. Nine hybrid promoters, verified by counting rows in the spreadsheet and cross-checked against 'nine hybrid promoters' in the text. Even multiplying by two hosts, three readouts and three replicates gives roughly 160 measurements - far under the ~1,500-row bar, and under the ~400 needed for classification.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially fits; the entire dataset is one small spreadsheet. Not the blocker.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Counts are consistent: the paper says nine hybrid promoters and the spreadsheet lists nine unique names. No disagreement between text and file.

a8_label_provenance.note: Not assessed as a blocker because there is no label column to trace. Noted for the record: the spreadsheet says transcription start site positions were predicted by a promoter-prediction tool, so those annotation columns are a model's output, but they are features here, not the target.

existing_models.name: Deep learning models of E. coli core promoter strength (Nucleic Acids Research 2025, gkaf863) and related transformer/CNN promoter-strength predictors
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported Pearson correlation around 0.87 for a transformer and 0.84 for a convolutional neural network on held-out synthetic promoter libraries; split details not checked since Part A already failed.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read in detail - the audit was stopped once Part A failed.

existing_models.name: Model-driven generation of artificial yeast promoters (Nature Communications 2020)
existing_models.score_and_split: Convolutional neural network ensemble trained on over 675,000 constitutive and 327,000 inducible yeast promoter sequences, R-squared above 0.79 on sequence-to-activity prediction.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read in detail - the audit was stopped once Part A failed.

backbone.name: Nucleotide Transformer or DNABERT-2 would be the natural DNA backbone for promoter sequences
backbone.hardware: CPU would suffice for 9 sequences, but fitting any head to 9 examples is meaningless.
backbone.licence: Not investigated; irrelevant given the row count.

integration.partner_dataset: Large synthetic promoter libraries already exist (over 675,000 yeast promoter sequences from the 2020 Nature Communications study; thousands of E. coli J-series and Trc variants), joinable on raw nucleotide sequence.
integration.join_key: Nucleotide sequence, or the standard iGEM J23 promoter part identifiers (J23117, J23118, J23119) present in the promoter names.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does a model trained on single-host promoter libraries predict which promoters stay equally strong in both a bacterium and a yeast - a question these nine promoters could at best spot-check, never train.

controls.positive_control: The paper's own weak/moderate/strong ordering of the three J23 promoters is a known hierarchy a model should recover, but nine points cannot establish it.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is runnable in principle but statistically empty at n=9.
controls.external_validation: Published single-host promoter libraries would serve, but only as a test set for a model trained elsewhere - this paper supplies no training data.

honest_claim_h3: Nothing beyond 'these nine specific hybrid promoters behaved as designed in two hosts'; no model fitted to nine sequences could claim anything that generalises, and the expression values are not even machine-readable.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a hybrid promoter's DNA sequence to predict how strongly it drives a gene in both bacteria and yeast.
plain_idea.train_on: The DNA sequence of each hybrid promoter, built from a yeast core promoter plus a bacterial promoter plus translation-start signals. Verified count: 9 promoters, which is the fatal problem.
plain_idea.predict: Expression strength in each host, and ideally the ratio between hosts. The true answer comes from red-fluorescent-protein readings by flow cytometry, messenger RNA levels by quantitative PCR, and an enzyme activity assay - but these exist only as bars in figures, not as numbers in any file.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Synthetic biologists who move metabolic pathways between hosts would like to pick a promoter that behaves the same in both, and nobody has modelled cross-host consistency. The data here is three orders of magnitude too small to attempt it.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: predict cross-kingdom promoter strength, or the bacteria-to-yeast expression ratio, from promoter sequence using a DNA language model with a frozen backbone and a small regression head. Dead on arrival - 9 promoters, and the expression values are not in any data file.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: the whole dataset is a 14 kB spreadsheet of 9 sequences, so compute is irrelevant. No cross-validation run is meaningful at this sample size.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in the one spreadsheet in the supplement. It took two minutes and returned 9, which kills the project outright.

verdict_reason: A small, well-executed synthetic-biology toolkit paper with no dataset behind it. Verified in the files: the entire supplement is a 22-page PDF plus one 14 kB spreadsheet listing 9 hybrid promoter sequences, built as three yeast core promoters crossed with three E. coli J23 promoters. That fails A5 (need ~1,500 rows, or ~400 for classification) by more than two orders of magnitude. It also fails A2 and A4: the prediction target - expression strength - appears nowhere as a column, only inside bar graphs in Figures 3-6, so the label would have to be reconstructed by digitising images, and no units are stated anywhere in the text. Separately, the task is already crowded: published promoter-strength models were trained on over 675,000 yeast and thousands of E. coli promoter sequences and report correlations around 0.84-0.87, so even the best case here would be a nine-point spot-check of somebody else's model.
